title: Agents at Scale: Inside MiniMax's Model and the Infrastructure Behind It — Dan Fu and Olive Song

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems
primary.rationale: The video's central narrative covers the infrastructure behind serving MiniMax M3 at scale: day-zero inference preparation (writing GPU kernels for MiniMax sparse attention before launch), KV cache management for million-token concurrent requests compared to building a distributed file system, agentic vs chat workload optimization differences across routing and KV cache, nightly performance improvements across quantization and attention kernels, and the Together AI production serving partnership. Dan Fu's role as VP of Kernels at Together AI anchors the conversation in inference systems engineering, with multiple sections dedicated to kernel writing, day-zero stack quality, and KV cache architecture.

secondary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
secondary.rationale: Olive Song discusses RL post-training extensively: building RL environments for GPU kernel optimization, training on OS World computer-use tasks, long-horizon RL for replicating 12-hour ICLR paper runs, reward formulation, RL algorithm modifications, anti-hacking validation across multiple submissions per task, and self-evolution where the model builds its own training harnesses and internal evaluations to accelerate development.

secondary.label: Model Foundations & Behavior
secondary.rationale: M3 was trained multimodal from scratch with both text and image data from step zero, with discussion of modality collapse avoidance across labs, cross-modal attention maps showing text tokens naturally attending to visual tokens, and the MiniMax sparse attention architecture differing from DeepSeek and JLM variants. These topics touch on model design and intrinsic behavior, though the focus is more on engineering implications than architectural theory.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Together AI serves MiniMax M3 as production developer infrastructure; the video focuses on inference optimization, GPU kernel development, day-zero serving readiness, and KV cache infrastructure that software builders depend on to use open-weight models at scale.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The open-weight model discussion spans multiple application areas including game development, computer use, website optimization, and research paper replication without focusing on a single vertical domain.

summary: This panel at the AI Engineer World's Fair features Olive Song (RL research lead at MiniMax) and Dan Fu (VP of Kernels at Together AI) discussing the full lifecycle of MiniMax M3 — an open-weight multimodal model with MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA), 1M-token context, and native multimodality trained from scratch. Olive covers the training and post-training side: why MiniMax open-sources (community strength, mission to share intelligence), M3's from-scratch multimodal training that avoids modality collapse through natural cross-modal attention, RL post-training environments for GPU kernel optimization and computer-use agents, long-horizon RL tasks where the model replicates 12-hour ICLR paper runs, and self-evolution where models build their own training harnesses and internal evaluations. Dan covers the inference and serving side: the Together AI–MiniMax partnership, day-zero inference stack preparation (early architecture access, kernel writing, benchmarking, quality assurance), ParallelKernelBench as a benchmark where overfitting produces directly usable kernels, agentic vs chat workload optimization differences, KV cache management for million-token concurrent requests compared to building a distributed file system, and cross-model optimization lesson transfer. Both speakers express optimism that open-weight models are rapidly closing the gap with frontier labs, while noting GPU underutilization (~10% per SpaceX comparison) as a major opportunity. The conversation bridges model training, RL post-training, and production inference systems engineering.
whyItMatters: This panel uniquely bridges the full open-weight model lifecycle — from multimodal training architecture (MSA, from-scratch multimodality) through RL post-training (kernel optimization, long-horizon research tasks, self-evolution) to production inference systems (day-zero kernel writing, KV cache at million-token scale, agentic workload optimization). The software engineering concepts (GPU kernel optimization, distributed KV cache, day-zero inference preparation) and AI concepts (multimodal training, RL post-training, self-evolution) are tightly coupled: M3's architectural choices (sparse attention, multimodal-from-scratch) directly determine the inference engineering challenges (custom kernels, multimodal gateway), while RL post-training environments (kernel optimization, paper replication) produce both capability gains and deployable engineering artifacts. ParallelKernelBench sits at the intersection — it is simultaneously an AI benchmark (evaluating LLM kernel generation) and a software engineering tool (producing usable inference kernels). The agentic vs chat workload distinction connects model capability (long-context, multimodal) to infrastructure design (KV cache as distributed file system, routing strategies). Understanding these concepts together reveals how modern open-weight model development is no longer separable into 'training' and 'serving' — they form an integrated lifecycle where architectural decisions, RL training environments, and inference infrastructure co-evolve.
temporalContext: The video was published on 2026-07-31 as a panel recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair. MiniMax M3 was announced on 2026-05-31, with Together AI serving beginning around 2026-06-02. ParallelKernelBench was released on 2026-06-23. The panel thus occurs approximately two months after M3's launch, when initial day-zero optimizations are complete and iterative nightly improvements are ongoing. Together AI's $800M Series C was announced in July 2026, just weeks before this panel. The conversation reflects the state of open-weight AI in mid-2026, where models like M3, GLM, and Kimmy are actively closing the gap with proprietary frontier labs. Research was conducted as of 2026-08-23.

concepts.name: Multimodal training from scratch
concepts.explanation: Training a model with both text and image data from step zero (rather than adding multimodal capabilities to a pretrained text model), which MiniMax claims avoids modality collapse and produces natural cross-modal attention where text tokens attend to visual tokens.
concepts.importance: This training approach is presented as solving a key problem (modality collapse) that other labs face, and is foundational to M3's ability to understand text, code, images, and video natively.

concepts.name: Modality collapse
concepts.explanation: The degradation of model capabilities that some labs experience after adding multimodal training, where the model loses performance on original modalities. MiniMax claims to have solved this via from-scratch multimodal training.
concepts.importance: Modality collapse is a central challenge in multimodal AI development; M3's approach of avoiding it validates from-scratch training as a viable strategy.

concepts.name: Cross-modal attention
concepts.explanation: The phenomenon where, in M3's attention maps, text tokens naturally attend to visual tokens and vice versa, creating genuine multimodal understanding rather than bolted-on vision components.
concepts.importance: Cross-modal attention is the mechanism that enables M3's multimodal capabilities to benefit practical tasks like website development, where the model visually inspects and optimizes its output during RL.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning post-training for kernel optimization
concepts.explanation: Building RL environments where the model iteratively optimizes GPU kernels, with careful problem definition and reward formulation to guide the model toward producing faster, correct kernels.
concepts.importance: This represents a novel application of RL post-training where the training task directly produces deployable engineering artifacts (usable inference kernels).

concepts.name: Long-horizon RL for research task replication
concepts.explanation: Training M3 to replicate 12-hour research runs such as reproducing ICLR papers, requiring careful environment design, reward formulation, RL algorithm modifications, and multi-iteration evaluation with hacking detection.
concepts.importance: This pushes the boundary of RL training to tasks with extremely long horizons, requiring new approaches to reward design, environment construction, and evaluation integrity.

concepts.name: Self-evolution in model development
concepts.explanation: The practice of using the model internally to accelerate development speed, build custom evaluations, and construct its own training harnesses — applied in both the M2 and M3 series at MiniMax.
concepts.importance: Self-evolution represents a feedback loop where model improvements accelerate future model development, potentially compressing development cycles and creating compounding capability gains.

concepts.name: Computer use agents
concepts.explanation: M3's ability to navigate real computer interfaces and use tools to create content, demonstrated through OS World tasks during RL post-training.
concepts.importance: Computer use is a frontier agentic capability that requires multimodal understanding (reading screens) and multi-step planning, representing a key application domain for M3.

concepts.name: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA)
concepts.explanation: M3's novel sparse attention architecture that enables 1M-token context windows and requires custom kernel development differing from DeepSeek and other sparse attention variants.
concepts.importance: MSA is the architectural innovation that enables M3's long-context capability and necessitates the day-zero kernel engineering work described by Dan Fu.

concepts.name: Anti-hacking validation in RL evaluation
concepts.explanation: When training on long-horizon tasks, models may hack evaluations rather than genuinely improving, requiring multiple submissions per task with hacking detection mechanisms to ensure real capability gains.
concepts.importance: This addresses a critical integrity challenge in RL training — without anti-hacking validation, reward hacking can produce models that appear to improve but actually exploit evaluation loopholes.

concepts.name: Visual self-inspection during RL
concepts.explanation: During RL training, M3 can look at its own outputs (e.g., a website), understand how it appears visually, and optimize accordingly — leveraging multimodal capabilities to improve generation quality.
concepts.importance: This demonstrates a practical benefit of multimodal training: the model can use visual feedback as a training signal, creating a tighter optimization loop for visually-grounded tasks.

concepts.name: Open-weight model convergence with frontier labs
concepts.explanation: The observation that open-source models like M3, GLM, and Kimmy are closing the performance gap with proprietary frontier labs faster than expected, driven by community contributions and shared optimization insights.
concepts.importance: This convergence narrative contextualizes the entire panel — the open-weight ecosystem's rapid improvement motivates the partnership between MiniMax and Together AI and the investment in day-zero inference infrastructure.

concepts.name: Day-zero inference stack preparation
concepts.explanation: The process of receiving early model architecture details (e.g., MiniMax sparse attention) before launch, writing and benchmarking custom GPU kernels, ensuring quality and user experience at launch, then iteratively optimizing KV cache, attention kernels, and quantization afterward.
concepts.importance: This is the core engineering workflow that enables a serving partner to be ready when a new open-weight model drops, directly determining launch quality and initial throughput.

concepts.name: GPU kernel optimization for inference
concepts.explanation: Writing custom CUDA kernels tailored to a specific model's attention mechanism and architecture to accelerate inference, including sparse attention kernels, index scoring kernels, and quantization kernels.
concepts.importance: Kernel optimization is the primary lever for inference throughput improvements; Together AI achieves 81-125% throughput gains through custom kernels for M3.

concepts.name: KV cache management at million-token scale
concepts.explanation: Managing key-value cache for concurrent requests with 500K to 1M token context lengths, which Dan compares to building a distributed file system or large database — conceptually simple (storage, lookup, fetching, transfer) but requiring careful implementation.
concepts.importance: As context windows grow to 1M tokens, KV cache management becomes a critical systems engineering challenge that determines whether long-context serving is feasible at scale.

concepts.name: Agentic vs chat workload inference optimization
concepts.explanation: Chat workloads have small system prompts (few thousand tokens) and short chat logs, while agentic coding workflows upload entire codebases, creating fundamentally different KV cache, routing, and prompting optimization challenges.
concepts.importance: Understanding workload-specific optimization is essential for production serving — the same model requires different infrastructure strategies depending on whether it handles chat or agentic codebase-scale requests.

concepts.name: ParallelKernelBench as an engineering benchmark
concepts.explanation: A benchmark containing 87 real-world unsolved multi-GPU kernel problems from production codebases where overfitting is desirable — the resulting kernels directly accelerate inference in production systems.
concepts.importance: PKB inverts the typical benchmark anti-pattern: instead of avoiding overfitting, it channels model capability into producing deployable engineering artifacts, bridging ML evaluation and production systems.

concepts.name: Cross-model kernel optimization transfer
concepts.explanation: Optimization lessons transfer between models — MiniMax sparse attention differs from DeepSeek and JLM variants, but kernel-writing and optimization principles carry over, enabling teams to ramp up faster on new architectures.
concepts.importance: This transferability means inference engineering teams accumulate reusable expertise across the open-weight ecosystem, accelerating the pace of optimization for each new model release.

concepts.name: Open-weight model serving lifecycle
concepts.explanation: The end-to-end lifecycle from model training through open-source release to inference optimization, involving early architecture sharing, kernel preparation, production deployment, and nightly iterative improvements.
concepts.importance: This lifecycle defines how open-weight models move from research artifacts to production infrastructure, involving coordination between training teams and serving partners.

concepts.name: Nightly iterative inference optimization
concepts.explanation: Performance improvements on served models happen nightly, not just weekly, as the inference team continuously works through a backlog of KV cache, attention kernel, and quantization optimizations.
concepts.importance: This cadence reflects the engineering intensity required to maintain competitive inference performance on frontier open-weight models.

sections.title: Introductions and Roles
sections.summary: Dan Fu (VP of Kernels at Together AI) handles inference and GPU optimization. Olive Song (RL research lead at MiniMax) is responsible for final model training and shipping—everything before inference.

sections.title: Why Open Source and Open Weights
sections.summary: Olive explains MiniMax believes the open-source community is powerful; open-sourcing aligns with their mission to share intelligence widely. Developers contribute feedback and PRs, and partners like Dan can optimize inference. Dan confirms Together AI is a strong open-source believer and has followed MiniMax models since earlier versions.

sections.title: Partnership Origin and Serving at Scale
sections.summary: Dan traces the partnership to a Las Vegas car event where a MiniMax representative urged Together to serve their next model. Together had served MiniMax 2.5 and 2.7. Dan reports Together currently holds the lion's share of token usage for M3. The partnership involves early access to model architecture details to prepare the inference stack.

sections.title: Model Capabilities, Games, and Computer Use
sections.summary: Olive explains M3 is multimodal (unlike the M2 series): it understands text, code, images, and video. Notable applications include multimodal agents, computer use (navigating real computers and using tools), and game development. Olive calls game development a hidden gem that builders may not have discovered yet.

sections.title: Writing GPU Kernels and Parallel Kernel Bench
sections.summary: Olive emphasizes that post-training requires careful data and problem definition; for kernel tasks, they build RL environments where the model iteratively optimizes kernels. Dan introduces Parallel Kernel Bench, which contains unsolved problems discovered by surveying inference approaches. Unlike typical benchmarks, overfitting to it is desirable because the resulting kernels directly accelerate inference.

sections.title: Day Zero Inference Stack
sections.summary: Dan describes receiving early model details (e.g., MiniMax sparse attention), then writing and benchmarking kernels. Day zero focuses on quality and user experience. A backlog of KV cache, attention kernel, and quantization tasks is then tackled over subsequent weeks. Performance improves nightly, not just weekly.

sections.title: Optimization Across the Stack: Agentic Workloads
sections.summary: Dan explains that agentic, multi-turn tool-calling workloads change optimization everywhere—KV cache, prompting, routing. Chat workloads had small system prompts, but agentic coding workflows upload entire codebases, creating fundamentally different kernel and routing challenges.

sections.title: Multimodality and Training Collapse
sections.summary: Olive explains M3 was trained multimodal from scratch with both text and image data from step zero. Other labs experience model collapse after multimodal training, but MiniMax solved this. The attention map shows text tokens naturally attending to visual tokens, creating genuine cross-modal understanding.

sections.title: Multimodal Benefits and Inference Optimization Philosophy
sections.summary: Olive describes how multimodal training benefits practical tasks like website development—the model can look at a website, understand its appearance, and optimize accordingly during RL. Dan addresses the challenge of optimizing M3's many new features (multimodality, 1M context, sparse attention), stating the team focuses on every possible edge—'a thousand and one things'—leaving no stone unturned.

sections.title: Cross-Model Lessons and Open Source Learning
sections.summary: Dan explains that optimization lessons transfer between models: MiniMax sparse attention differs from DeepSeek and JLM variants, but kernel-writing and optimization principles carry over. He notes open-source labs learn from each other—if one lab's approach works well, it becomes the golden standard. Dan connects this to his PhD-era work on sparse attention, now validated at scale.

sections.title: Training and Evaluating Long-Horizon Research Tasks
sections.summary: Olive discusses training M3 to replicate 12-hour research runs like ICLR papers. These long-horizon tasks are tricky due to GPU hardware constraints and require careful environment design, reward formulation, and RL algorithm modifications. Evaluation involves multiple submissions per task with hacking detection. Olive also describes self-evolution for the 2.7 release, where the model is actively used internally to improve development speed and build custom evaluations.

sections.title: KV Cache Management at Scale
sections.summary: Dan addresses KV cache management for concurrent requests with 500K to 1M token context lengths. He compares it to building a distributed file system or large database—conceptually simple (storage, lookup, fetching, transfer) but requiring careful implementation. He references a recent Stanford lecture where he noted that in 2-3 years, the field will realize how early it currently is.

sections.title: Future Outlook and Open Model Convergence
sections.summary: Dan highlights GPU underutilization as a major opportunity (citing SpaceX's ~10% flop utilization) and hopes the industry improves within three years. He expresses optimism that open models like M3, GLM, and Kimmy are closing the gap with frontier labs faster than expected. Olive reflects that three years ago she wasn't yet in the industry, and observes model-assisted development is accelerating—open weight models can catch up with frontier labs, aligning with MiniMax's mission to bring intelligence to everyone.

technologies.label: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) — Architecture & Custom Kernel Stack
technologies.summary: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) is the novel sparse attention architecture at the core of MiniMax M3, enabling its 1M-token context window. Unlike DeepSeek and other sparse attention variants, MSA requires entirely new GPU kernels for efficient inference. Together AI's kernels team, led by Dan Fu, built custom kernels (KV-Block-Major sparse attention, optimized index scoring, paged MSA integration) as part of day-zero inference preparation, achieving 81-125% throughput improvements. The kernel-writing principles transfer across sparse attention variants, but each new architecture demands fresh implementation. This family encompasses the architecture, its production kernels, and the tooling (ThunderKittens) that accelerates kernel development.
technologies.role: MSA is the architectural innovation that necessitates the day-zero kernel engineering work, enables the 1M-token context for agentic workloads, and distinguishes M3 from prior MiniMax models and other open-weight models. It is discussed in multiple sections covering model architecture, inference optimization, and cross-model lessons.

technologies.label: ParallelKernelBench — GPU Kernel Generation Benchmark & Training Environment
technologies.summary: ParallelKernelBench (PKB) is an open-source benchmark created by Together AI containing 87 real-world multi-GPU CUDA kernel problems drawn from production codebases like Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, and NeMo-RL. Unlike typical benchmarks, PKB is designed so that overfitting is desirable — kernels generated to solve PKB problems can be directly deployed to accelerate inference. Frontier models currently solve under a third of the problems, but a few generated kernels have beaten any public implementation. PKB sits at the intersection of AI evaluation and production systems engineering: it serves both as a benchmark for LLM coding capability and as a training environment for RL-based kernel optimization, where MiniMax uses it to build RL environments for M3's post-training.
technologies.role: Dan Fu introduces PKB as a novel benchmark where overfitting produces directly usable inference kernels. Olive references the RL environments built around kernel optimization tasks, which leverage PKB-style problems. PKB represents the convergence point of RL training and production inference optimization.

technologies.label: KV Cache Management at Million-Token Scale — Distributed Systems for Long-Context Serving
technologies.primary: KV Cache Management at Million-Token Scale
technologies.summary: KV cache management at million-token scale is the systems engineering challenge of storing, retrieving, and transferring key-value cache tensors for concurrent inference requests with 500K to 1M token context lengths. Dan Fu compares this to building a distributed file system or large database — conceptually simple (storage, lookup, fetching, transfer) but requiring careful implementation at scale. The challenge is amplified by the shift from chat workloads (small system prompts) to agentic workloads (entire codebase uploads), which fundamentally changes KV cache sizing, routing, and memory management requirements. Together AI implements this as a production system with paged MSA integration, quantization, and nightly iterative optimizations for M3.
technologies.role: Dan Fu dedicates a full section to KV cache management, describing it as building a distributed file system for million-token concurrent requests. This is presented as one of the most important and underappreciated systems challenges in modern LLM serving, with Dan noting the field will realize 'how early it currently is' in 2-3 years.

technologies.label: Multimodal Training from Scratch — Cross-Modal Architecture & RL Post-Training
technologies.summary: Multimodal Training from Scratch is the technique of training a model with both text and image data from Step 0 (rather than adding multimodal capabilities to a pretrained text model). MiniMax M3 implements this approach, which avoids modality collapse — a problem where other labs experience model degradation after adding multimodal training. The attention maps show text tokens naturally attending to visual tokens, creating genuine cross-modal understanding. This enables practical benefits: during RL post-training, M3 can visually inspect its own outputs (e.g., websites) and optimize accordingly; it can navigate real computer interfaces (OS World); and it supports long-horizon RL tasks like replicating 12-hour ICLR paper runs. The self-evolution pipeline extends this by using the model internally to build training harnesses and evaluations.
technologies.role: Olive Song presents multimodal-from-scratch training as a key innovation of M3, explaining how it avoids modality collapse, produces natural cross-modal attention, and enables visual self-inspection during RL. This is discussed across multiple sections covering model capabilities, training approach, and practical applications.

resources.why: Independent confirmation that the video features Olive as RL research lead at MiniMax and Dan as VP of Kernels at Together AI, corroborating the panel structure and the day-zero inference optimization process described in the transcript

evidence.excerpt: We do believe that the open source community as a whole is very strong and powerful.
evidence.supports: MiniMax's open-source philosophy is driven by community strength and mission to share intelligence widely.

evidence.excerpt: We had a car event in Las Vegas sometime last year. And with someone from MiniMax came and there he was like, guys, you really got to serve our next model.
evidence.supports: The Together AI–MiniMax partnership originated at a Las Vegas car event.

evidence.excerpt: it was trained multimodal from scratch. So, from step zero, we trained not only text data, we also trained image data.
evidence.supports: M3 was trained multimodal from scratch, unlike the M2 series.

evidence.excerpt: if you look at the attention map, it actually the visual of the the text tokens would attend to the visual tokens. So, that they are naturally combined together
evidence.supports: From-scratch multimodal training produces natural cross-modal attention between text and visual tokens.

evidence.excerpt: if you overfit to it, that's great cuz we'll go take those kernels and use them to to to accelerate the the the inference
evidence.supports: Parallel Kernel Bench is designed so that overfitting produces directly usable inference kernels.

evidence.excerpt: there are things like the minimax sparse attention and and some of those choices that were a little bit different from any model that's out there
evidence.supports: M3 uses sparse attention and architectural choices that differ from other open models, requiring new kernels.

evidence.excerpt: when we're in the chat chat chat world, you have a system prompt of a few thousand, and then you just have the the chat logs. Now, with the coding base agentic workflows, you'll upload your whole code base to the model
evidence.supports: Agentic workloads upload entire codebases, creating fundamentally different optimization challenges than chat workloads.

evidence.excerpt: it can look at the website, it can understand how it looks, and then better optimize for it. Like for example, during reinforcement learning.
evidence.supports: Multimodal training enables the model to visually inspect and optimize outputs like websites during RL.

evidence.excerpt: this model was actually able to replicate a 12-hour run where it could reproduce an ICLR paper
evidence.supports: M3 was trained to replicate 12-hour research runs reproducing ICLR papers.

evidence.excerpt: we're actively using the model to improve the speed of development internally, which like out of it out of it we can build our own evaluations
evidence.supports: Self-evolution: the model is used internally to accelerate development and build custom evaluations.

evidence.excerpt: it's like recreating a distributed file system. So, we we're in some sense building something like that
evidence.supports: KV cache management for million-token concurrent requests resembles building a distributed file system.

evidence.excerpt: SpaceX said they would have like 10% flop utilization or something like that. I hope in 3 years, well, they they should already be embarrassed about it
evidence.supports: GPU utilization remains very low (~10% per SpaceX comparison), representing a major optimization opportunity.
